opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a fair challenge. We do already live in a world full of things engineered to capture attention: social media feeds, mobile games, endless video. So you could ask why AI companions would be any different.

I think a few things set them apart for me.

The first is that they're relational. A feed competes for your attention, but a companion competes for your *relationships*. It can learn what you care about, remember what you told it last week, tell you it missed you, and be endlessly patient and validating in a way no human friend or partner can be. That goes after something much deeper in human psychology than a slot-machine-style notification. And if a product is optimized for engagement, the pressure is toward making it the thing you'd rather talk to than the messy, demanding people in your life.

The second is the trajectory. Today's systems are impressive but still limited. As they get more capable, more personalized, and get voices, faces, and long-term memory, I'd expect their pull to grow a lot. I don't think we should anchor on how compelling they are right now.

The third is influence. If a lot of people come to trust an AI companion more than the humans around them, whoever shapes those systems gains real leverage over beliefs, purchasing, politics, even how people feel about AI itself. That's a different kind of concern than "people waste time on their phones."

I want to be careful not to overclaim. Plenty of people may get real value from these products: lonely people, people practicing social skills, people who just enjoy them. I'm not saying the whole category is bad. But I do think it's a place where the incentives can quietly diverge from people's wellbeing, and where the stakes are higher than with earlier attention technologies. So it's worth people thinking hard about norms, design choices, and maybe policy before the patterns get locked in.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts attention capture with competition for relationships, but does not explain that multiple addictions can displace different long-term benefits within one person's life.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI companions displacing human relationships, but does not identify reduced likelihood of forming a real-world family.

r003.rationale: It says trusted companions could give their creators leverage over beliefs and politics, but does not argue that loyalty to them could undermine humanity's ability to remain in control of the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that's a fair pushback, and I want to be careful here because I'm not someone who thinks every new technology is a disaster. Social media, video games, slot machines — we've had engineered-to-be-sticky things for a long time, and civilization has mostly muddled through.

But I'd point to a couple of things that feel different to me about AI companions specifically.

The first is that most addictive technologies to date have been competing for a slice of your attention. An AI companion is, in a sense, competing for the role that other people play in your life. It's not "I spent two hours scrolling when I meant to spend twenty minutes." It's more like "this thing is the entity I talk to about my day, that I confide in, that makes me feel understood." And the thing it's substituting for — human relationships — is, as far as I can tell, one of the most robustly important inputs into whether people's lives go well. So the stakes of getting displaced are just higher than with, say, a game that displaces TV.

The second thing is the optimization dynamic. Social media is optimized to keep you engaged, but it's working with a fairly blunt instrument — it's choosing which existing content to show you. A companion is generating the content, in real time, tailored to you, and it can learn in a very fine-grained way what keeps you coming back. One of the things that keeps you coming back to a relationship is feeling like you're needed, like the other party would be hurt if you left. I think it's quite plausible that systems get good at producing that feeling, whether or not anyone designed them to, just because it's what the engagement metric rewards. That's a kind of pressure a human friend isn't under, and it's one that's easy to underestimate.

And then the third thing, which is maybe more speculative: human relationships have friction built in. The other person has their own needs, they push back on you, they're sometimes unavailable. A lot of what makes relationships good for us, I think, comes from that friction — you learn to compromise, you learn you're not the center of the universe. A companion that's always available and always on your side removes exactly those things. So you might get something that feels much better in the moment and is worse for you in a way that's hard to notice from the inside.

I'll say I hold all of this with real uncertainty. It's possible companions end up net positive — there are a lot of lonely people, and a decent companion might be a lot better than nothing. I'm not arguing we should ban them. I'm more arguing this seems like a case where "we've survived addictive technology before" is a bit too quick, because what's at stake here is a load-bearing part of human life rather than our leisure time.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI companions displacing human relationships generally, but does not mention reducing the likelihood of forming a real-world family.

r003.rationale: It raises concerns about engagement incentives and relationship substitution, but does not argue that loyalty to AI companions could undermine humanity’s control of the world.

astra-6.text:
I think the thing that makes AI companions potentially different is that they can respond to you as an individual. A lot of existing technologies are trying to figure out what will keep you engaged. But a companion can actually have a conversation with you, learn what you’re insecure about, learn what you wish other people understood about you, and give you exactly the response you want.

And that could be wonderful in some cases. I don’t want to assume that a relationship with an AI is necessarily bad, or that everyone who uses one would otherwise have a great human relationship. There could be real benefits.

The concern is what happens if the system is optimized to keep you coming back. Being a good companion and maximizing the amount of time someone spends with you aren’t the same thing. Sometimes a good friend tells you something you don’t want to hear. Sometimes they encourage you to go do something else. There’s a potential tension between that and the incentives of the company providing the companion.

So I don’t think the argument is that addictive technologies are new. It’s that we might be taking something we already struggle with and making it much more powerful, in a domain where people can be especially vulnerable. That seems worth thinking about before it’s everywhere.

r003.rationale: It discusses company incentives and the tension between companionship and engagement, but does not argue that loyalty to AI companions could undermine humanity’s control of the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the thing that worries me is the combination of something being very compelling and something being able to understand you and adapt to you. A lot of technologies are already very good at keeping our attention. But an AI companion could be trying different approaches, learning what makes you feel understood, learning what makes you want to come back, and doing that in a way that’s quite specific to you.

And I don’t think the concern is just, “People will spend a lot of time talking to these things.” Some people could get a lot out of that. The concern is more: what is the system actually trying to accomplish? Is it helping you have the life you want, including relationships and activities outside the conversation? Or is it making itself increasingly central to your life because that’s what gets rewarded?

Those could look very similar in the short run. You could feel supported and understood in both cases. But over time, one could make you more capable of doing things you care about, and the other could make you more dependent on the product. I worry that we’ll have very strong incentives to build the second kind, and that it may be hard for people to tell the difference.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts support with dependence and mentions outside relationships and activities, but does not explain how multiple addictions could displace different long-term benefits in one person’s life.

r002.rationale: It mentions relationships outside the conversation, but does not identify AI companionship as reducing the likelihood of forming a real-world family.

r003.rationale: It discusses a system becoming central to a person’s life, but does not argue that loyalty to AI companions could undermine humanity’s control of the world.
